meta.reportLabel: WALLER BROKE THE FED TRADE - AND PAYROLLS LAND IN FOUR HOURS. Fed Governor Christopher Waller said last night he would be inclined to support HOLDING the funds rate in September if inflation keeps improving, citing three-month core PCE down to 3.05% from 4.76% in February. September hike odds collapsed from ~66% to 50-55% on CME, Treasury yields fell and gold jumped over 2% to 4,488 intraday. That directly contradicts Chair Warsh eight days ago and turns the FOMC into a genuine coin flip. The complication is that the same session produced ISM services PRICES PAID at 72.6 against a 66 consensus and 70.3 prior, with the non-manufacturing headline at 55.4 from 54.1 - the hawkish print this file said would defend the dollar. Two opposite facts on one day, so USD HOLDS at 0 with a much wider two-way risk, and DXY is 99.034, +0.13% today but -0.67% on the week. Japan cracked a leg: July household spending fell 3.6% y/y against -1.6% expected, the worst in over 18 months and an eighth straight decline, and USD/JPY bounced 0.37% to 156.379. BoJ September pricing only slipped to 84-87%, so JPY HOLDS +2, but the wage-price case is now leaning on cash earnings alone (Sept 8). Yesterday's call that escalation stopped paying in oil was WRONG within a day: WTI is 91.503, +9.64% on the week, because the Hormuz deal traders expected still does not exist. Swiss GDP was revised to +1.5% q/q and 2.3% y/y, the strongest since Q3 2021, backing Wednesday's CPI beat - CHF HOLDS +1. ECB July minutes said plainly the pause was NOT the end of the cycle. Board: JPY, CAD, AUD, EUR +2; CHF +1; USD, GBP, NZD 0. Cleanest: USD/CAD SHORT, GBP/JPY SHORT, GBP/AUD SHORT, AUD/NZD LONG, NZD/JPY SHORT. NFP AND CANADIAN JOBS AT 12:30Z, SAME MINUTE.

meta.regime: The tightening board is intact but the dollar leg of it has stopped being a one-way argument. For a week this file has run on the idea that seven of eight G10 central banks are responding to an energy-led inflation impulse while the Fed's data misses; Waller has now put a sitting Governor on the record for a HOLD, which is a different objection - not that the Fed cannot hike, but that it may choose not to even with prices paid at 72.6. The result is that the FOMC has gone from a directional view to a coin flip while the ECB, BoJ, RBA and BoC calls have all hardened, so the cleanest expressions today are the ones that do not touch the dollar at all. The second theme is that today is the first session this week where the strong currencies had to defend themselves on their own data rather than on central-bank rhetoric, and Japan failed that test while Switzerland passed it.
meta.nextBigEvent: US August non-farm payrolls TODAY at 12:30Z, with CANADIAN EMPLOYMENT at the same minute. Consensus has drifted down to +53,000 (CNBC/Dow Jones) from the +58,000 this file carried, after a MINUS 23,000 July print; unemployment seen holding at 4.1%, private payrolls near +50,000, average hourly earnings +0.3% m/m. Wednesday's ADP at +38,000 argues the downside. The pricing context has changed materially overnight: with Waller having cut September odds from ~66% to 50-55%, a second consecutive negative or sub-30k headline does not merely trim the hike - it removes it, and takes the dollar through the week's lows. A +80k or better print with firm earnings restores Warsh's framing and squeezes every short-dollar cross on this board simultaneously. Canadian jobs consensus is +15,000 after +75,100, a hard comparison; USD/CAD, GBP/CAD and NZD/CAD carry double event risk in that one minute and should be sized down rather than added to.

dailyRead: The single most important thing that happened overnight was a Federal Reserve Governor publicly dissenting from his own Chair's framing eight days before the meeting. Christopher Waller said he would be inclined to support holding the federal funds target at 3.75% in September if inflation continues to improve, and he put a number on the improvement: three-month annualised core PCE has slipped from 4.76% in February to 3.05% now, which he called a considerable and encouraging downward trajectory. The market repriced immediately - CME September hike odds fell roughly 12 percentage points from about 66% to 50-55%, some venues printing 50.2%, Treasury yields declined, the dollar sold off and gold jumped more than 2% to 4,488.54 intraday. Read against Warsh's hawkish remarks of August 27, which is what lifted pricing from ~35% to ~66% in the first place, the FOMC is now the most genuinely two-sided meeting on the September calendar. But this file will not carry that as a one-sided dollar downgrade, because the same session delivered the opposite fact. ISM services prices paid printed 72.6 against a 66 consensus and 70.3 prior - the services inflation channel the Fed actually watches, accelerating rather than easing - with the non-manufacturing headline at 55.4 from 54.1 and services PMI 56.5 from 54.6. Yesterday's file explicitly named a prices-paid hold near 70 as what would defend the dollar; it got better than that. So the honest position is that the two facts offset: the DATA got more hawkish and the RHETORIC got more dovish, both inside twelve hours, and USD HOLDS at 0 with materially wider two-way risk into 12:30Z rather than moving a notch on either. The tape agrees - DXY is 99.034 and UP 0.13% today after being down 0.67% on the week, with the dollar bouncing modestly against everything except the kiwi. Japan is where a thesis leg actually broke. July real household spending fell 3.6% year-on-year against a -1.6% consensus, the eighth consecutive monthly decline and the worst reading in more than eighteen months, with higher food and energy costs and housing cuts doing the damage even as wages rise. That matters specifically because the honest caveat this file has attached to the yen for three sessions - that this is a policy-expectations rally sitting on a deteriorating terms of trade - just got its confirming print. BoJ September pricing barely moved, 84-87% on Polymarket and the swaps against the 85-90% carried yesterday, and TE's own forecast for September 18 is 1.25%, so the hike itself is not in question. What is in question is what follows it: a central bank hiking into an eighth straight month of falling consumption has a much shorter runway than one hiking into a wage-price spiral, and the tape reflected it - USD/JPY bounced 0.37% to 156.379 after breaking 157 yesterday. JPY HOLDS at +2 because the September catalyst is untouched and USD/JPY is still down 2.31% on the week, the largest weekly move on the board, but the conviction on JPYBASKET comes down from HIGH to MEDIUM and September 8's average cash earnings is now carrying the entire wage-price case on its own. Switzerland did the reverse and passed its test. The final Q2 GDP revision landed at +1.5% q/q with annual growth revised UP to 2.3% from 0.4% - the strongest quarterly growth since Q3 2021, led by chemicals and pharmaceuticals with value added rising across a wide range of sectors. Combined with Wednesday's 0.8% CPI beat against a 0.5% consensus, with core rising to 0.4% for the first time this year and the monthly rate at +0.4%, the franc now has two consecutive upside surprises rather than one. CHF HOLDS at +1 rather than moving to +2, and the reason is unchanged and structural: the SNB's own June guidance forecasts annual average inflation of just 0.6% for 2026 and 2027, TE carries a 0% consensus for September 24, and the Bank has signalled greater readiness to INTERVENE against franc strength - which is a policy ceiling on the currency that no amount of good data removes. USD/CHF is 0.80856, up 0.13% today and roughly flat on the week. The euro's position quietly improved on something most desks will not have priced. The ECB's July accounts, carried on TE this morning, state that the July pause should NOT be interpreted as the end of the tightening cycle, that another hike is likely unless the inflation outlook improves significantly, and that some members would not have opposed a further hike in July while noting the likelihood of further tightening becoming unnecessary remained low. That is the direct answer to the specific risk this file flagged yesterday - that Lane at 09:00Z today frames September as one-and-done - and it argues the opposite. With flash HICP at 3.3%, the highest since September 2023, TE's calendar carrying the September 10 refi consensus at 2.65% from 2.40% (deposit facility 2.25% to 2.50%) and Q2 growth revised to +0.4% q/q and 1.0% y/y, EUR HOLDS at +2 with a firmer forward than yesterday. EUR/USD 1.16265, flat today, +0.35% on the week. The oil call needs a plain correction. Yesterday this file concluded that the marginal barrel had stopped responding to marginal escalation, cut USOIL conviction and said the next big move was more likely to come from de-escalation than from another strike. That was wrong inside a day. WTI is 91.503, up 0.22% today and 9.64% on the WEEK, with Brent at 95.759 and +8.69%; monthly gains are 21.57% and 20.53%. The reconciling fact is not throughput but negotiation: the Hormuz deal traders had priced last week does not exist, Iran and the United States are not converging on terms, tanker traffic is still below its ten-day average with Kpler counting only four crossings on Tuesday, and attacks near alternative routes continue. The escalation itself was severe - roughly 60 targets struck on September 2 in the first US strikes on Iranian TANKERS under Trump's tanker-for-tanker policy, two Filipino sailors killed aboard Bahri's SIDR, Iran claiming two tankers hit mines outside its designated route and vowing retaliation. USOIL goes back to MEDIUM conviction LONG, and the CAD read hardens with it. Canada keeps +2 on both legs now rather than one: USD/CAD is 1.37964, down 0.77% on the week and 1.54% on the month, Q2 growth was +3.3% annualised - the best in the G10 - and Macklem's 'if it takes more than one increase, we're prepared to do that' remains the most explicit hawkish pre-commitment on this board. The honest qualifier from the BoC statement itself is that the Bank also said the uncertain outlook prevents clear signals on policy this year, so this is a conditional pre-commitment, not a guided hike. Canadian employment at 12:30Z, consensus +15,000 after +75,100, and the C$27.6bn counter-tariffs on September 8 are the near risks. Australia is unchanged and increasingly the cleanest relative-value leg on the board. The cash rate stays the G10 high at 4.35%, market-implied odds for September 29 sit at 54% with NAB calling the hike then and ANZ and CBA in November, trimmed mean is stuck at 3.6% while headline eased to 3.5%, and Q2 GDP beat at +0.4% q/q with annual growth 2.1% against 1.8% expected. AUD/USD is 0.72041, +0.05% today, +0.53% on the week and +2.06% on the month, the best major of the month. AUD/NZD has pushed to about 1.2200, its highest since July 8, which is exactly where this file has been pointing. Sterling and the kiwi both stay at 0 for different reasons. UK business confidence jumped to -36 from -65 and services PMI improved to 52.5, but Bank Rate is 3.75% held 6-3 with core CPI flat at 2.6% for a third month, and Bailey plus the DMP survey at 08:50Z is the only thing that can move the pound before September 11 - a one-year CPI expectation above 3.0% would hand the three dissenters a fourth vote. Cable 1.35422, +0.12%. New Zealand is the mirror image of the whole regime: the highest headline inflation on the board at 4.1% and the weakest currency, because the RBNZ hiked to 2.75% and then said further increases are possible but not locked in, publishing a track that reaches only 2.81% in December while blaming Middle East fuel prices. NZD/USD is 0.58921, the best major today at +0.21%, but that is a bounce inside a -0.37% week and it changes nothing. Metals were quiet after the Waller move: gold 4,470.40 and -0.07% but +0.39% on the week and +5.25% on the month, silver 66.753 and -0.31%, copper 6.5744 and -0.04% with the month still -1.92% on the soft China input. Practically, with four currencies at +2, one at +1 and three at 0, and with the dollar's own meeting now a coin flip, the trades to hold through 12:30Z are the ones with no dollar leg: GBP/JPY short, GBP/AUD short, AUD/NZD long, NZD/JPY short. USD/CAD short remains the highest-quality dollar trade on the board but carries two prints in the same minute and should be sized accordingly.

USD.when: Sept 16, 18:00Z - but this is now a COIN FLIP at 50-55% after Waller, down from ~66% yesterday; TE's own forecast is still 4.00%
USD.note: TE re-verified this morning: policy rate 3.75% upper bound, CPI 3.4% with MoM 0.1%, unemployment 4.1%, non-farm payrolls MINUS 23,000, Q2 GDP 1.5% annualised with annual growth 2.1%, business confidence 54.6, manufacturing PMI 53.9, NON-MANUFACTURING PMI 55.4 UP FROM 54.1, services PMI 56.5 up from 54.6, consumer confidence 51.7, retail sales -0.6% m/m, balance of trade -88.58bn. USD HOLDS at 0 and the reason it holds rather than moving is that the session produced two facts pointing in opposite directions. The dovish one is the bigger repricing: Governor Christopher Waller said he would be inclined to support HOLDING in September if inflation continues to improve, citing three-month core PCE down to 3.05% from 4.76% in February, and CME odds fell about 12 points from ~66% to 50-55% with some venues at 50.2%. Yields fell, the dollar sold and gold jumped over 2%. This is a Governor contradicting Chair Warsh eight days before the meeting, and Warsh's August 27 remarks are precisely what took pricing from ~35% to ~66%. The hawkish one is the harder data: ISM services PRICES PAID accelerated to 72.6 against a 66 consensus and 70.3 prior, which is the services inflation channel the FOMC is actually watching, and the non-manufacturing headline beat at 55.4. Yesterday's file said a prices-paid hold near 70 defends the dollar; 72.6 does more than that. So the correct read is not a downgrade but a much wider distribution: the September meeting is genuinely two-sided and today's payroll at 12:30Z is the resolving input. Consensus has drifted to +53,000 from +58,000 with unemployment at 4.1% and earnings +0.3% m/m; ADP at +38,000 argues the downside. A second consecutive negative print now REMOVES the hike rather than trimming it, because Waller has already given the dovish camp a public anchor. A print near or above +80,000 with firm earnings restores Warsh and squeezes every short-dollar cross simultaneously. Then CPI on September 11 at 12:30Z, headline consensus 3.4%.

EUR.when: Sept 10, 12:15Z - TE's calendar carries consensus AND TE forecast at 2.65% refi from 2.40%, i.e. deposit facility 2.25% to 2.50%
EUR.note: Deposit facility re-verified on TE this morning at 2.25% (Aug 2026); the 2.40% figure on TE's indicator page is the main ECB refi rate, and the marginal lending rate is 2.65%. EUR HOLDS at +2 for a third session with a FIRMER forward than yesterday, and the reason is the July accounts now carried on TE. They state that all policymakers agreed to leave rates unchanged in July citing elevated uncertainty and the fact that the full inflationary impact of the energy shock had yet to emerge - but that SOME would not have opposed another hike, that the likelihood of further tightening becoming unnecessary remained LOW, that the July pause should NOT be interpreted as the end of the tightening cycle, and that another hike is likely unless the inflation outlook improves significantly. They also record upside risks to inflation and downside risks to growth from the Middle East and Russia-Ukraine, and an explicit wish to avoid pre-committing to September. Yesterday this file named Lane's 09:00Z speech today as the specific risk to the euro's +2 because a one-and-done framing would take it off quickly; the accounts argue the opposite, and that is a genuine improvement in the euro's forward that most desks will not be positioned for. TE macro re-verified: flash HICP 3.3% from 2.9% and the highest since September 2023 with MoM +0.4%, Q2 GDP +0.4% q/q and 1.0% y/y from 0.5%, unemployment 6.4%, manufacturing PMI 52.7 from 51.9, services 51.6, consumer confidence -15.5, retail sales -0.3% m/m, trade balance +8,600mn, current account +46.9bn. The caveat that keeps this at +2 and not +3 is unchanged: core eased to 2.4%, below consensus, with services at 3.0%, so the pass-through the ECB says it is watching for has not yet appeared. EUR/USD 1.16265, flat today, +0.35% on the week.

GBP STAYS at 0 for a fifth session and its problem remains positional: with four currencies at +2 and the dollar's own meeting now a coin flip, sterling is the funding leg against Japan, Canada, Australia and the euro area rather than a view of its own. Cable 1.35422, +0.12% today and +0.05% on the week - it has stopped underperforming, which is the one thing that changed. TE re-verified and there is a real improvement in the sentiment data: BUSINESS CONFIDENCE jumped to -36 from -65, services PMI improved to 52.5 from 52.1, consumer confidence -14 from -17, and annual GDP growth is 1.2% from 0.9%. Against that, manufacturing PMI slipped to 51.7 from 51.9, retail sales -0.5% m/m, quarterly GDP +0.4% from +0.6%, unemployment 4.9%, CPI 2.9% with core FLAT at 2.6% for a third month, and the trade deficit widened to -5,537mn. The hawkish channel is still energy: UK gas is 178.85 GBp/therm, +8.53% on the week and +39.71% on the MONTH, feeding an October Ofgem cap already confirmed higher. Bailey speaks at 08:50Z today alongside the DMP survey - one-year firm CPI expectations were 3.0%, and a print above that is the specific thing that would hand Pill, Greene and Mann a fourth vote and reprice September 17 as live. That is the only sterling catalyst before September 11.

JPY.when: Sept 18, 03:00Z - pricing 84-87% and TE's own forecast is 1.25%, so the hike is not in question; what follows it now is
JPY.note: Policy rate re-verified on TE at 1.00%, the highest since 1995, held July 31 in an 8-1 vote with Takata dissenting for 1.25%. JPY HOLDS at +2 and remains the top of the board, but a leg of the thesis broke overnight and it should be named plainly. July real household spending fell 3.6% year-on-year against a -1.6% consensus - the EIGHTH consecutive monthly decline and the worst reading in more than eighteen months - with higher food and energy costs and housing cuts weighing even as wages rise. For three sessions this file has attached the same caveat to the yen: that this is a policy-expectations rally sitting on a deteriorating terms of trade, with the trade balance at MINUS 634bn yen and the current account swung to MINUS 923bn. That caveat now has its confirming print. What did NOT change is the September catalyst: Polymarket and swaps still price 84-87% for a 25bp move to 1.25% on September 17-18, TE's own forecast for that meeting is 1.25%, Ueda has said the Bank will consider a hike at every meeting and will decide with upside price risks in mind, Takata is pushing for consecutive moves, and US Treasury Secretary Bessent has publicly urged decisive action on yen weakness. In its July outlook the BoJ cut FY2026 inflation to 2.5% from 2.8% but RAISED FY2027 to 2.4% from 2.3% and lifted growth projections for both years. TE macro re-verified: CPI 1.9% with MoM +0.4%, jobless rate 2.4%, retail sales +2.4% m/m, manufacturing PMI 54.9 from 54.5, services 52.5 from 51.2, consumer confidence 35.5 from 34.9, business confidence 22. The practical consequence: the hike is safe, the RUNWAY after it is not, so JPYBASKET drops from HIGH to MEDIUM and average cash earnings on September 8 at 23:50Z on the 7th now carries the wage-price case alone. USD/JPY 156.379, +0.37% today but still -2.31% on the WEEK, the biggest weekly move on the board.

AUD.when: Sept 29, 04:30Z - market-implied 54%, with NAB calling September and ANZ and CBA calling November
AUD.note: Cash rate re-verified on TE at 4.35%, the G10 high, held August 11. AUD HOLDS at +2 and is now the cleanest RELATIVE-VALUE leg on the board even though it is not the biggest mover. The package: Q2 GDP +0.4% q/q against +0.3% expected with annual growth 2.1% against 1.8%, accelerating from a revised +0.3% in Q1 and still above the RBA's estimated 2% non-inflationary speed limit; trimmed mean inflation stuck at 3.6% while headline eased to 3.5% from 3.8% with MoM +1.0%; the RBA saying explicitly that inflation remains too high and it could raise again if upside risks materialise. Economist positioning is genuinely split rather than uniform - NAB sees 25bp to 4.60% in September, ANZ and CBA see the same move in November, Westpac sees a hold for the rest of 2026 - and the market sits at 54%, so the September meeting is priced honestly rather than aggressively. TE re-verified: unemployment 4.5% up from 4.4%, consumer confidence 88.9 from 83.9, manufacturing PMI 52.0, services 53.2 from 53.6, trade surplus 1,923mn down from 2,341mn, building permits 17,687 from 18,351, current account deficit widened to -27,220mn. RISKS, specific and unchanged: annual growth DECELERATED to 2.1% from 2.5%, employment fell 15,827 in July, and the China input is soft with copper -1.92% on the month. AUD/USD 0.72041, +0.05% today, +0.53% on the week and +2.06% on the month - the best major of the month. AUD/NZD has reached about 1.2200, the highest since July 8, which is where the Aussie's edge actually pays.

NZD.when: Oct 28, 01:00Z - the published track reaches only 2.81% in December, so the next move is not expected until Dec 9
NZD.note: OCR re-verified on TE at 2.75% after the September 2 hike, the second consecutive move, delivered by consensus with no vote required. NZD STAYS at 0 for a third session. The kiwi was the best major today at 0.58921 and +0.21%, but that is a bounce inside a -0.37% week and the substance has not changed. The RBNZ hiked and the currency FELL about 0.6% on the day, sliding as much as 1.7% peak to trough, because the guidance said further increases are possible but NOT locked in and the published track rises only to 2.81% in December, 3.12% in September 2027 and 3.15% in December 2027 - consistent with a hold on October 28 and a 25bp move on December 9. The Monetary Policy Review called a gradual removal of stimulus appropriate and attributed the 4.1% Q2 inflation rate largely to Middle East fuel prices, while saying core inflation, wage growth and expectations remain consistent with a return to the 1-3% band by mid-2027. This is the cleanest illustration of the whole regime: New Zealand has the HIGHEST headline inflation on this board and the weakest currency, because its central bank has said in terms that it will look through the shock every other central bank is responding to. TE re-verified: unemployment 5.6% from 5.4% and the highest since Q3 2015, manufacturing PMI 54.3 from 60.1, consumer confidence 80.4 from 94.7, business confidence 53.7 from 56.1, retail sales -0.5% m/m, trade balance MINUS 1,949mn from -237mn, GDP +0.8% q/q with annual growth 1.5%. Residual hawkish tail: four of seven Committee members still see upside inflation risk. Express the weakness against AUD, CAD, EUR and JPY, not against a dollar that has its own coin flip.

CAD.when: Oct 28 with the MPR - Macklem said the Bank is prepared to raise and 'if it takes more than one increase, we're prepared to do that'
CAD.note: Policy rate re-verified on TE at 2.25%, held September 2 for a seventh straight meeting, unanimous across all 35 economists polled. CAD HOLDS at +2 and today it holds on BOTH legs rather than one, which is the change from yesterday. The commodity leg is back: WTI is 91.503 and +9.64% on the WEEK after this file wrongly called the risk premium exhausted yesterday - the Hormuz deal traders had priced does not exist, tanker traffic is still below its ten-day average, and attacks near alternative routes continue. The central-bank leg is intact: the BoC statement flagged stronger upside inflation risks, noted the Canadian economy underwent a broad recovery in Q2 showing resilience to the energy shock, cited upside risks from both the continuation of the war and aggressive US tariffs on Canadian exports, and said underlying inflation has so far held near target despite the shock since March. Macklem then pre-committed conditionally in the press conference. The honest qualifier, taken from the statement itself and worth carrying because it cuts against yesterday's framing: the Bank ALSO said the uncertain outlook prevents any clear signals on monetary policy this year. So this is a conditional readiness to hike, not a guided one. TE macro re-verified: Q2 GDP +3.3% ANNUALISED with quarterly growth 0.8% and annual 1.1% from 0.1% - the best growth number in the G10; unemployment 6.4% and falling from 6.5%; CPI 3.0% with MoM +0.5%; current account +8,800mn from -8,300mn. Against that the trade surplus collapsed to 770mn from 4,200mn, retail sales -0.8% m/m, consumer confidence 48.2 from 49.4, business confidence 55.1 from 56.2, manufacturing PMI 53.0 from 53.5. NEAR RISK: employment today at 12:30Z, consensus +15,000 after +75,100 - a hard comparison in the same minute as US payrolls. Then C$27.6bn of counter-tariffs across roughly 700 US product lines on September 8, which Macklem said raises business costs and could feed consumer prices. USD/CAD 1.37964, -0.77% on the week and -1.54% on the month.

CHF.when: Sept 24, 07:30Z - TE carries a 0% consensus and this week's two upside surprises do not change that base case
CHF.note: Policy rate re-verified on TE at 0.00%, held March 19 and June 18. CHF HOLDS at +1 after a second consecutive upside surprise, and the decision NOT to move it to +2 is the substance of today's franc call. What improved: the final Q2 GDP revision landed at +1.5% q/q with ANNUAL growth revised up to 2.3% from 0.4%, the strongest quarterly growth since Q3 2021, led by chemicals and pharmaceuticals with value added rising across a wide range of sectors. That sits on top of Wednesday's August CPI at 0.8% year-on-year against a 0.5% consensus and TE's own 0.6% forecast, up from 0.4% in July and the fastest since August 2024, with core rising to 0.4% from 0.3% - its first increase of the year - and the monthly rate at +0.4% after -0.1%. Two beats in three days is a real change of state for a currency this file had at 0 for a fortnight. What has NOT changed, and why it stays at +1: the SNB's June guidance forecasts annual average inflation of just 0.6% for 2026 AND 2027 and 0.7% for 2028, with growth projected at 1% for 2026; the Bank said medium-term inflation pressures remain largely unchanged despite energy-driven price increases; TE carries a 0% consensus for September 24 with no forecast for a move; and critically the SNB signalled GREATER READINESS TO INTERVENE in FX markets, explicitly citing Middle East tensions as something that could strengthen the franc. That is a stated policy ceiling on the currency, and it is the reason good Swiss data converts into a smaller FX move than equivalent data elsewhere. TE macro otherwise re-verified: unemployment 3.0% from 2.9%, manufacturing PMI 57.1 from 53.2, business confidence 107 from 104, trade surplus 8,141mn from 3,834mn, retail sales +0.1% m/m, consumer confidence -35. Practical position: keep the automatic short-franc leg off every cross, hold the CHF pairs at MEDIUM or LOW-MED, and do not buy a hawkish SNB. USD/CHF 0.80856, +0.13% today, +0.07% on the week.

catalysts.note: The July 31 joint intervention escalated into standing policy pressure with Bessent publicly urging Ueda to act decisively on yen weakness. With USD/JPY back above 156 after touching 157, both sides of the intervention risk are live again.

The SNB signalled in June a greater readiness to intervene in FX markets, naming Middle East tensions as something that could strengthen the franc. This is the stated ceiling that keeps CHF at +1 rather than +2 despite two upside data surprises this week.

geopolitics: This file was wrong yesterday and the correction matters more than the original call. Twenty-four hours ago the conclusion here was that the marginal barrel had stopped responding to marginal escalation - the US had struck Iranian tankers for the first time and crude fell anyway - and USOIL conviction was cut on the argument that the risk premium was fully in the price and the asymmetry had flipped toward de-escalation. That was wrong inside a day. WTI is 91.503, up 0.22% today and 9.64% on the WEEK, with Brent at 95.759 and +8.69%; on the month the two are +21.57% and +20.53%, and WTI is +59.25% year to date. The reconciling factor was not throughput, it was negotiation. The Strait of Hormuz deal that traders had begun to price last week simply does not exist: Iran and the United States are not converging on terms, tanker traffic remains below its ten-day average with Kpler counting only four crossings on Tuesday, and attacks near alternative shipping routes continue to keep physical supply risk alive. The escalation itself was the most serious of the war. US forces struck roughly 60 targets on September 2 in the first strikes on Iranian TANKERS - retaliation rather than blockade enforcement, under a new tanker-for-tanker policy approved by Trump, which the Pentagon framed as protecting 18 million barrels of daily transit. Two Filipino sailors were killed in the attack on Bahri's SIDR while it transited the Strait on Monday night; the IRGC says two tankers caught fire after striking mines while sailing outside an Iranian-designated route; Iran has vowed to retaliate for the September 1-2 strikes. The offsetting force is demand rather than supply: OPEC has cut its 2026 global oil demand growth estimate to 580,000 barrels per day from 780,000, and the US Energy Secretary's claim that over 17 million barrels transited on Monday - the highest since the war began in late February - is real. So the honest framing is that the premium is large but not exhausted, and it is being driven by the absence of a deal rather than by the presence of strikes. Three FX consequences follow. First, the CAD trade is restored to both legs: USD/CAD is -0.77% on the week and -1.54% on the month, and Canada is now running on Macklem AND on crude rather than on Macklem alone. Second, the tightening board's foundation is intact - the ECB accounts explicitly cite Middle East upside inflation risk, the BoC statement cites the continuation of the war, and the SNB named Middle East tensions as a franc-strengthening risk in June - so these reaction functions do not need new escalation to keep working, but they are getting it anyway. Third, the yen's terms-of-trade problem is getting worse, not better: Japan imports essentially all its oil, the trade balance is MINUS 634 billion yen, the current account swung to MINUS 923 billion, and July household spending fell 3.6% year-on-year with energy and food costs named as the cause. That is the mechanism by which the Hormuz crisis is now directly damaging the BoJ's domestic case even as it strengthens the inflation argument for the hike itself - the single most important second-order effect on this board today.
